title: Giants bringing in Terrion Arnold for visit, legal troubles and all
description: Giants bring in ex-Detroit Lion Terrion Arnold.
fullText:
The New York Giants, who were without three of their top five cornerbacks at practice on Tuesday, will host former Detroit Lions cornerback Terrion Arnold for a free-agent visit on Wednesday, a source confirmed.

Arnold, a 2024 first-round pick by the Detroit Lions, was released on June 29. Arnold, 23, isfacing eight felony charges stemming from allegations he orchestrated the abduction and beating of three men. The Lions released him after he was charged.

The Associated Press summarized the reason for the charges against Arnold this way:

In June, prosecutors in Florida said Arnold arranged for the men to be pistol-whipped after he wrongly suspected them of stealing $100,000 in cash and luxury goods from him. Police called him the "primary conspirator" in the February attack, and a judge set his bail at $1 million.

According to Pro Football Talk, a conviction could result in a life sentence for Arnold. The legal troubles have not prevented NFL teams from looking into signing Arnold. He has already visited with the New Orleans Saints, Seattle Seahawks, and Houston Texans.

Slot cornerback Dru Phillips, who has a knee sprain, has not practiced since late last week. Greg Newsome (knee) has been out of practice this week. Multiple reports indicate Paulson Adebo did not practice on Tuesday.

The Giants have signed defensive backs J.T. Woods, David Long, and D.J. James during the past week.

title: Pirates pull Paul Skenes from start vs. Marlins after just 65 pitches
description: The Pittsburgh Pirates lifted ace Paul Skenes from the game after five innings and just 65 pitches.
fullText:
The Pittsburgh Pirates caused a bit of a stir Tuesday night when they lifted starter Paul Skenes after just 65 pitches.

It marked the fifth-shortest outing of Skenes' career by pitch count.

The Pirates' ace, who has been battling to find his Cy Young form in the second half of the season, exited after five innings with the Pirates down 2-0 to the Miami Marlins.

Skenes gave up a home run to Esteury Ruiz in the bottom of the third inning, then his fifth inning unraveled a bit when he hit Ruiz with a pitch. Ruiz would score the next batter, racing around from first to score thanks to shortstop Jacob Gonzalez's throwing error.

Skenes' last pitch of the night was nearly a home run, with Bryan Reynolds coming up with the robbery to end the inning and keep the score 2-0.

Bryan Reynolds with ANOTHER home run robbery this year

What a catch pic.twitter.com/VyU3ga4Upc

But Skenes did not come back out for the sixth inning, yielding to Yohan Ramirez.

The Pirates have not provided any public updates on if Skenes' removal was injury related.

title: Fever coach Stephanie White unloads on WNBA critics: 'Go to hell'
description: Stephanie White pushed back on criticism surrounding DiJonai Carrington's hard foul and blasted online "hate" and "divisiveness" overshadowing WNBA.
fullText:
Indiana Fever coach Stephanie White spent her pregame news conference Tuesday denouncing "the hate, the fear mongering (and) the divisiveness" hijacking the league, vitriol that reached a boiling point over the weekend after DiJonai Carrington committed a hard foul against Sophie Cunningham on Aug. 8.

"It's a shame we can't have an opportunity to talk about what great basketball they're playing because they are (expletive) playing," White said during an impassioned speech ahead of the Fever's game against the New York Liberty. "Every day these women put their ass on the line. Love will win. Grace will win. Humility will win, and kindness will win."

White concluded her speech, "I will always stand by them. Everybody else can go to hell."

Stephanie White made the following statement before tonight's game: pic.twitter.com/VkYThRldsu

White opened her pregame news conference by addressing the Flagrant 2 foul called on Chicago's Carrington, who was subsequently ejected from the Fever's win over the Sky on Aug. 8 for making "unnecessary and excessive" contact with Cunningham's neck.

Immediately after the incident, White said officials made "the right call" in her postgame remarks, adding she didn't think Carrington intentionally fouled Cunningham. White coached Carrington for two seasons in Connecticut from 2023-24 and said Carrington is known for "play(ing) her butt off."

"(Carrington's) going to compete. Nobody's going to go walking in for a layup," White said Aug. 8. "And so I don't oppose the hard foul, but I also don't think that she intentionally went for the neck."

On Tuesday, White shot down any claims she didn't have her player's back and clarified she hadn't properly seen a replay of the foul before she spoke postgame.

"For those who have anything to say about the play in the last game, I didn't see the play in real time. I went straight to a press conference," White explained Tuesday. "I thought the play got called right. Thankfully, Sophie's okay. Was it egregious? Absolutely. When you have a chance to watch that over and over and over on replay, you can see that. I didn't have that in real time."

White added, "An online community (is) trying to create narratives that simply don't exist. Trying to create a fabrication or distortion of who I am, of what I'm about... I take personally any suggestions that I don't 100% always have my players' back. I ride with them 10 toes down all the time. All of the time. They know that. Our players' success, our players' health and wellness, our players' safety is always a top priority for me. One of the things I pride myself on is my relationship with players."

White said the toxic online commentary dominating headlines has overshadowed the amazing basketball that's taking place day in and day out, which she called "a shame."

"We are united. We are connected. We will not be divided," White said.

title: 49ers coach reveals vague plan for playing time in preseason opener
description: San Francisco 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan gave a rough outline for the team's playing time distribution in their preseason opener vs. the Titans.
fullText:
San Francisco 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan on Tuesday revealed the outline of his team's plan for playing time in their preseason opener against the Tennessee Titans on Thursday.

The 49ers and Titans held a joint practice Tuesday leading up to an off day Wednesday. Typically under Shanahan the 49ers have used a joint practice as the "preseason" work for the starters, and then the game is for reserves and players trying to carve out roster spots. Shanahan said the team has a plan for Thursday's game, but didn't dish out exact details.

Unsurprisingly, he did mention the team's starters aren't in line to play much.

"We have, but we haven't told any of the players yet," Shanahan said. "There won't be many starters playing. We'll see with injuries today and stuff. That doesn't mean none, but we've got to balance that out. We haven't told the players yet, so wait until we do that with them this afternoon."

Players like Nick Bosa and Christian McCaffrey who were both out of Tuesday's session lead a group of players unlikely to suit up. It would be a surprise if left tackle Trent Williams and quarterback Brock Purdy played. Wide receiver Mike Evans and linebackers Fred Warner and Dre Greenlaw should also get the night off Thursday. The other players who don't play should give us a good indicator of where they stand in the hunt for roster spots or starting jobs.

A handful of potential starters who will likely play Thursday include the entire rookie class. Wide receiver De'Zhaun Stribling has a real chance to be one of the team's top two receivers in Week 1. Offensive lineman Carver Willis and linebacker Jaden Dugger are also rookies who could wind up in starting roles. We'll be keeping a close eye on the rookies since how they respond in a game will have a significant impact on their respective trajectories in Year 1.

title: LSU QB Sam Leavitt says foot injury is no longer on his mind
description: The Tigers signal caller appears to have put his injury behind him.
fullText:
LSU Tigers quarterback Sam Leavitt is putting his foot injury firmly in the rearview mirror ahead of his debut season in Baton Rouge.

Speaking about his recovery with the media, Leavitt acknowledged that the first several months were challenging, particularly after undergoing a second surgery to have the pins removed from his foot. He now has no hardware remaining and said the recovery process taught him an important lesson in patience.

"Delayed gratification was a big thing for me," Leavitt said.

Leavitt explained that he initially expected his foot to quickly return to normal after the second surgery, but the recovery did not happen as quickly as he anticipated. Instead, he had to trust the process, continue working and figure out with LSU's medical staff what was preventing his foot from progressing.

Once they identified the issue, Leavitt said his recovery took a significant step forward.

"Then it kind of just like popped from there," he said. "And it's just been incredible."

Now, Leavitt said the injury rarely crosses his mind when he steps onto the field. He still has to warm up his foot before practice and maintain his nightly routine, but otherwise, he feels like his old self.

"I really don't think about it out on the field at all," Leavitt said.

The LSU quarterback went a step further, saying he is currently at 100% and has been for the past few months.

That is encouraging news for the Tigers as Leavitt prepares for the 2026 season. After spending the offseason recovering and adjusting to his new surroundings, he can now focus entirely on developing within LSU's offense and preparing for the season.

Leavitt also made sure to credit LSU's medical staff for helping him through the recovery process.

"I'm 100% right now," Leavitt said. "Just want to show a lot of love to Dallas and the whole staff just constantly grinding, getting me back."

After months of uncertainty and rehabilitation, Leavitt appears ready to move forward without the injury being a major factor in his preparation.

title: Dave Roberts issues warning to Andy Pages ahead of Royals game
description: Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts had a warning for Andy Pages during their current series against the Kansas City Royals.
fullText:
Andy Pages is undoubtedly one of the best players on the Los Angeles Dodgers. Now in his third season with the organization, he has fully broken out.

He earned his first All-Star selection for his performance both in the batter's box and defensively in the outfield. Across 118 games, he has posted a .270 batting average, .337 on-base percentage, .794 OPS, 19 home runs and 76 RBIs.

MORE: Dodgers All-Star reacts to wife's personal announcement during MLB season

However, Pages does have his flaws, and the biggest problem he has had this year involves one of MLB's biggest changes, the Automated Ball-Strike system.

Pages has challenged 24 total pitches this season and has been successful just 11 times, a 46% success rate that falls below the league average of 48%.

He has also routinely challenged pitches early in games at moments where the run expectancy does not change much even if the call is overturned, making the challenges feel wasteful rather than strategic.

His ABS decisions have started to frustrate manager Dave Roberts, who issued a warning before Tuesday's game against the Kansas City Royals, according to Jack Harris of the California Post.

Roberts and the coaching staff have addressed several players, including Pages, about ABS challenge usage. Roberts also admitted the team is weighing whether they could potentially ban individual players from challenging altogether if the results do not improve.

His comments make sense considering how the league has adapted to the ABS system. According to Baseball Savant, catchers have had a significantly higher success rate at 59% when challenging pitches.

Banning hitters, especially ones who struggle with identifying the right moment to challenge, could be a smart approach moving forward.

title: A’s slugger Nick Kurtz could miss the rest of the season with a thumb injury
description: Athletics first baseman Nick Kurtz may be in danger of missing the rest of the season because of his injured right thumb.  Manager Mark Kotsay told reporters before his team’s game against Tampa Bay on Tuesday that Kurtz needs to be in a brace for four weeks following a platelet-rich plasma injection on Aug. 4.  Kotsay alluded to the fact that four weeks without mobility for Kurtz could make a return before the end of September difficult to envision.
fullText:
WEST SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — Athletics first baseman Nick Kurtz may be in danger of missing the rest of the season because of his injured right thumb.

Manager Mark Kotsay told reporters before his team's game against Tampa Bay on Tuesday that Kurtz needs to be in a brace for four weeks following a platelet-rich plasma injection on Aug. 4. Kotsay alluded to the fact that four weeks without mobility for Kurtz could make a return before the end of September difficult to envision.

Kurtz, 23, went on the injured list with a sprained right thumb on July 11 and returned two weeks later. He struggled at the plate following his return, going 1 for 18 in seven games. Kurtz was expected to see a hand specialist in Los Angeles last week.

The reigning AL rookie of the year is batting .256 with 21 home runs and 69 RBIs in his second season in the majors. Kurtz, a native of Lancaster, Pennsylvania, was selected as an All-Star but unable to participate in Philadelphia because of the injury.

title: Arianna Huffington says even high-flying CEOs are unhappy and feel stuck in their multimillion-dollar jobs: ‘It’s a trap’
description: Huffington Post's multimillionaire founder Arianna Huffington says success is a ‘trap’—CEOs with big salaries are afraid to leave jobs they no longer love
fullText:
It's every worker's dream: You work hard and climb the ladder until eventually you're rewarded with an executive title and cushy salary to go with it. But according to Huffington Post founder Arianna Huffington, the reality isn't quite as glamorous as it looks—and plenty of CEOs, she says, are desperate to quit, despite seemingly having it all.

"Success can be a trap," Huffington told Fortune, adding that once you've dedicated years of your life to honing your craft and gaining recognition, it can feel impossible to leave it all behind and start something new. Even if you're miserable where you're at.

"It's a trap because a lot of very successful people have a hard time leaving," she explained. "I have CEO friends who've stopped loving their jobs, but they're afraid to leave."

And it's not just the huge mortgages, private school fees and luxury first-class vacations they've become accustomed to bankrolling with their multi-million dollar pay packages keeping them stuck.

"The financial trap is much easier to see, while the identity trap is less tangible but no less real," Huffington added. "They're so identified with the CEO role, or the anchor of an evening show, or whatever big job comes with a lot of recognition—it's become their identity."

Huffington spent a grueling 11 years building Huffington Post into one of the biggest names in digital media, growing its newsroom to more than 850 journalists and becoming the first digital-native outlet to win a Pulitzer Prize. She graced the covers of magazines, made Time's list of most influential people and was a regular at the likes of Davos.

"There are no guarantees anytime you start a new company," the 76-year-old multimillionaire said. "But I was ready to throw myself into health, and if I hadn't done it, I would have kind of betrayed myself."

At the time, when she was weighing up whether to hold onto what she had built or walk away, Huffington said that her mother's voice was in her head.

"She brought me up not to be afraid of failing," she said, adding that women in particular are hit harder by perfectionism and therefore more likely to remain stuck and not take that leap of faith in case it doesn't work out. "My mother used to say failure is not the opposite of success, it's a stepping stone to success."

title: The 20 best college towns where life revolves around their universities, ranked
description: College towns offer student experiences that set them apart from big cities. Life in Ann Arbor revolves around the University of Michigan's culture.
fullText:
College towns offer unique student experiences that set them apart from big cities.

For many, large research universities anchor the local economy and culture.

Ann Arbor tops the list of best college towns, driven by the University of Michigan's rich culture.

For many students, college is a time filled with rigorous classes, internship applications, and energy-drink-filled all-nighters.

College towns often offer a unique experience that helps these students manage flourishing social lives and hobbies alongside their academic careers.

Business Insider looked at some of the cities and towns across America where students can thrive, and compiled a list that best matches the loose definition of a college town.

To do so, we used data from the Census Bureau's latest population estimates and from WalletHub's 2025 ranking of the best college towns. We then filtered out major cities, focusing instead on places where colleges and universities anchor the local economy and lifestyle.

Not all college towns are built the same, however, and while some are extensions of nearby metropolises, others are smaller communities tucked away from other urban areas.

School: Brigham Young University

Nestled between mountains in the Utah Valley, the city of Provo is home to the private Brigham Young University, which has a student population of over 35,000 students.

The town has a lively economy, a young population, and its local culture is closely tied to religion and sports. Locals often enjoy the city's unique access to hiking trails and stunning natural landscapes.

School: University of Tennessee — Knoxville

Home to the University of Tennessee — Knoxville and its over 40,000 students, the city of Knoxville is a vibrant and energetic community.

The city is considered a gateway to the Great Smoky Mountains — as it's located less than an hour away from unique Appalachian landscapes — and a hub for country music, which soundtracks the city's scene.

During gamedays, over 100,000 fans pack into the school's Neyland Stadium in their best orange-and-white attire.

Located between Austin and Houston, College Station, Texas, is one of the state's best college towns. The city's culture, economy, and lifestyle are shaped by Texas A&M University.

The land-grant, SEC university has one of the largest student populations at its College Station campus, with over 72,000 students.

School culture unites the city, with Aggie pride inescapable on gamedays as fans congregate at the school's Kyle Field, which seats over 100,000.

The city is also home to the George H.W. Bush Presidential Library and Museum.

17. Chapel Hill, North Carolina

School: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

The school's roughly 34,000 students shape local culture and economy. Along with Durham — home to Duke University — and Raleigh — home to North Carolina State University — Chapel Hill is part of North Carolina's Research Triangle, a region where tech and education are among the most popular fields of employment.

Thanks to the college's prevalence and the region's entry-level job opportunities, the town has a highly educated, uniquely young population.

School: Michigan State University

Neighboring the state capital of Lansing, the city of East Lansing combines college culture with government employment.

The city is home to roughly 52,000 students at Michigan State University, which dominates local culture and sports. The school's sprawling campus sits directly across the city's downtown. Restaurants, cafés, shops, and bars cluster around the university.

15. San Luis Obispo, California

School: California Polytechnic State University.

Halfway between San Francisco and Los Angeles, the town of San Luis Obispo combines the energy of a college town with the laid-back lifestyle of California's Central Coast.

The over 20,000 students at Cal Poly have easy access to the region's beaches, mountain trails, and wine country, while the city's compact downtown is filled with restaurants, shops, and nightlife.

School: University of Connecticut

Population: 15,979 (per the 2020 census)

In the small community of Storrs, which is surrounded by the forests and farmland of northeastern Connecticut, the University of Connecticut is the center of life.

Downtown Storrs, located next to campus, has more than 70 businesses, as well as nature preserves and hiking trails. The university's size gives the otherwise rural community a steady stream of restaurants, events, arts programming, and student activity, especially during UConn basketball game days.

School: Harvard University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology

Few American cities have an academic identity as strong as Cambridge. With Harvard and MIT anchoring higher education in the city, the opportunities available attract thousands of students, researchers, and academics from around the world.

Harvard Square mixes restaurants, shops, museums, and entertainment around Harvard's historic campus, while Kendall Square, beside MIT, has become a hub for jobs in technology, biotechnology, and startups.

The city's location across the Charles River from Boston also gives students easy access to the metropolis's jobs, nightlife, and culture via public transit.

The University of Georgia's historic campus sits directly across from downtown Athens, making the city one of the most recognizable college towns in the South.

Athens has a prominent music scene that produced famous bands like R.E.M. and the B-52s, and live music remains a major part of the city's identity. Its walkable downtown is packed with local restaurants, bars, coffee shops, boutiques, and music venues.

On fall weekends, Georgia Bulldogs football takes over the city as tens of thousands of fans pack Sanford Stadium.

School: Washington State University

Tucked among the rolling hills of southeastern Washington, Pullman is a small town where Washington State University defines local culture and identity.

The compact downtown is within walking distance of campus and has many locally owned restaurants, coffee shops, and retailers.

The city's remote location contributes to a close-knit student and faculty community. School traditions and Cougar sports play a major role in local identity, which is also influenced by the natural landscape that surrounds the city.

School: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign

The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign spans the neighboring cities of Champaign and Urbana and is home to one of the Midwest's largest college communities, with over 59,000 students.

The university's research focus also extends to the local economy, with its Research Park and business incubator supporting technology companies and startups, and drawing students to remain in the area for internships and jobs long after graduation.

Located on Wyoming's high plains between mountain ranges, Laramie combines a historic Western downtown with the culture of the state's flagship university.

The over 10,000 students at the University of Wyoming have easy access to hiking, mountain biking, climbing, skiing, and other outdoor activities in the surrounding mountains and forests.

The city's downtown adds restaurants, coffee shops, breweries, and local businesses within a relatively compact area near campus, and the college culture also spans museums, performing arts, and Wyoming Cowboys athletics.

Purdue University's large student body of nearly 58,000 makes West Lafayette one of the most university-driven communities in the Midwest.

The school's reputation in engineering, science, and technology contributes to a local economy centered on research and innovation, while Big Ten athletics give the city's culture a strong sense of school spirit.

School: University of California, Berkeley

UC Berkeley's academic reputation and history of student activism have helped shape the city's culture for generations.

Just south of campus, Telegraph Avenue remains one of the city's most distinct student districts, with streets lined with independent stores, restaurants, and record shops.

Students can also head into the Berkeley Hills to explore beautiful trails and parks or easily reach San Francisco and other Bay Area communities through public transportation.

School: University of Wisconsin—Madison

Built between two lakes, Madison gives students a unique mix of a major state capital, a large Big Ten university, and easy access to the outdoors.

The city's State Street serves as the main connector between campus and the Wisconsin State Capitol, with cafés, restaurants, bars, galleries, and shops lining the corridor. On warm days, students gather along Lake Mendota at the university's Memorial Union Terrace.

College sports, cycling, lake activities, farmers markets, and a strong local food scene keep the city lively year-round.

Schools: Florida State University, Florida A&M University

Florida's capital city has one of the largest and most varied student communities on this list, anchored by multiple public colleges.

Florida State University and Florida A&M University each bring distinct traditions to the city, and along with the local Tallahassee State College, the city has a student population of over 65,000.

FSU's Seminoles generate major football weekends around Doak Campbell Stadium, while FAMU, one of the country's most prominent historically Black universities, has its own deep academic, cultural, and athletic traditions.

The city is also the center of the Florida state government and offers plenty of opportunities for students interested in politics, public policy, law, and government.

Located in the center of North Florida, Gainesville is home to the University of Florida's over 63,000 students, along with thousands of researchers, Gators fans, and university employees who give the city a unique college-town identity.

The city is surrounded by nature preserves, forests, and freshwater springs where locals can swim, kayak, and tube, while the downtown area has a growing restaurant, craft beer, and arts scene that keeps students busy year-round.

College football is especially important to local culture, with home games drawing dozens of thousands of fans to the school's Ben Hill Griffin Stadium throughout the fall.

The University of Virginia shapes Charlottesville's deep academic and historic identity, while the surrounding Blue Ridge foothills give the city easy access to some of Virginia's most scenic landscapes.

The university's campus sits near a lively corridor of restaurants and shops, while the pedestrian Downtown Mall serves as a center for dining, shopping, and live entertainment.

The surrounding region is also known for its unique wineries, farms, and natural mountain scenery.

School: Arizona State University

Arizona State University's sprawling Tempe campus gives the city a distinctly youthful energy within the larger Phoenix metropolitan area.

Historic Mill Avenue, directly beside campus, is lined with restaurants, bars, shops, and entertainment venues, becoming a major center of student activity at night.

The school's focus on research, technology, and entrepreneurship also bolsters Tempe's economy, while the city's location within the Phoenix metro area gives graduates access to one of the Southwest's largest job markets.

School: University of Michigan-Ann Arbor

Home to the University of Michigan and its over 50,000 students, Ann Arbor is the best and most distinct college town in the US.

College culture is deeply woven into the city's landscape, where campus buildings blend into a walkable downtown filled with restaurants, bookstores, cafés, bars, and cultural institutions.

Few traditions dominate the city like Michigan football, which attracts over 100,000 fans to Michigan Stadium during fall Saturdays, while maize-and-blue crowds fill the surrounding streets and businesses.

The unique combination of college sports, a lively downtown, a major research university, and a strong cultural scene makes Ann Arbor one of the country's quintessential college towns and ranks it at the top of this list.

title: Trump administration finalizes ownership reporting exemption for US firms
description: Aug 11 () - The Trump administration on Tuesday finalized a rule exempting U. companies and individuals from ‌reporting beneficial ownership information to the Treasury Department's financial ‌crimes ...
fullText:
Aug 11 (Reuters) - The Trump administration on Tuesday finalized a rule exempting U.S. companies and individuals from ‌reporting beneficial ownership information to the Treasury Department's financial ‌crimes unit, rolling back reporting requirements established under a 2021 law aimed ​at combating illicit finance.

The Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, will still require foreign reporting companies to disclose beneficial ownership information for foreign individuals, the department said in a ‌statement.

"Treasury is eliminating a ⁠burdensome reporting requirement for millions of law-abiding business owners without compromising our national security," Treasury ⁠Secretary Scott Bessent said in the statement.

Beneficial owners are defined as anyone who has an ownership interest of at least 25% ​in a ​business or someone who exerts "substantial ​control" over the entity.

FinCEN ‌had previously implemented rules requiring certain companies to report beneficial ownership data as part of anti-corruption and anti-money laundering efforts backed by lawmakers and the Treasury Department under former President Joe Biden.

The Treasury Department said that FinCEN will delete previously ‌reported information by Americans from the ​government's beneficial ownership information database.

Under the ​rule finalized on Tuesday, ​foreign companies would not be required to ‌report Americans who helped those foreign ​companies register ​to do business in the United States.

It also exempts foreign pooled investment vehicles registered in the United States from ​reporting the beneficial ‌ownership information of a U.S person in control of ​the investment vehicle, the Treasury Department said.

title: More than 1,200 people arrested during recent Atlanta ICE operation
description: A recent ICE push in Atlanta led to more than 1,200 arrests. Of those, 720 people have some form of criminal history, the agency said.
fullText:
More than 1,200 undocumented immigrants were arrested throughout Georgia over the past few weeks as part of what the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials are calling an "enhanced immigration enforcement operation."

The operation, called "Operation Safe Community — Atlanta" was intended to "net" undocumented immigrants who have criminal histories. Charges ranged in severity from drug crimes and DUIs to aggravated assault and crimes against children, according to the agency. Only half of those arrested, however, had any criminal history.

"Our officers did what they do best: they arrested and removed dangerous criminal offenders from American communities," ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations Acting Assistant Director Patricia Hyde said in an Aug. 7 statement. "Removing these criminal alien offenders from Georgia neighborhoods makes for much safer communities, and that is exactly what the men and women of ICE work to accomplish every day across our great nation."

A total of 1,226 undocumented immigrants were arrested as part of the operation in Georgia, ICE said. Of those, 720 individuals had been convicted or charged with a crime in the United States.

Additionally, five individuals were arrested from the same address, which belonged to a trucking company ICE says is "known for employing" undocumented immigrants.

Hyde said while only half of the arrests were of those with criminal histories, "make no mistake, every one of the (undocumented immigrant) offenders apprehended during this operation was in violation of U.S. immigration law."

ICE officials released the names and charges of nine individuals, hailing from Mexico, El Salvador, Romania and Honduras. Other names and charges were not released.

Many immigration cases and violations are civil violations and not criminal acts, according to Berardi Immigration Law.

Overstaying a visa, violating the terms of a visa, or simply existing while undocumented are civil offenses. While they may still result in deportation or removal, these violations have typically been handled through civil court and have not included jail time.

Other offenses, like smuggling, reentering the U.S. after a removal, or using fraudulent documents on immigration paperwork, are criminal offenses that can carry significant jail time, especially on top of prior charges.

Earlier this summer, the Department of Homeland Security scrapped a plan that would have brought two ICE detention centers to Georgia. A large 10,000-bed detention facility was planned for the town of Social Circle, while a 5,000-bed processing facility was planned for the town of Oakwood.

After months of backlash in both communities (including protests, town hall meetings, and Social Circle cutting off water to their warehouse), both projects were scrapped, and the warehouses that had already been purchased by DHS were made available to other federal agencies.

"The City of Social Circle has received notification from Congressman Mike Collins that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is no longer pursuing an ICE detention facility within the City of Social Circle. This information is based on confirmation from multiple sources within DHS," Social Circle officials said in a June 18 statement. "Based on the information provided to the City, it is our understanding that the property could be sold if there are no other federal agencies that express interest in the property. While the exact process has not been confirmed, it is anticipated that any sale would occur through the General Services Administration (GSA)."

Both warehouses were purchased significantly above fair market value, and the properties have yet to be returned to the local tax base.

Oakwood officials said at the beginning of July they were still waiting on their own official confirmation from DHS, but it is their understanding the Oakwood facility will fall under the same designation as Social Circle.

Irene Wright covers immigration in Georgia as the Atlanta Connect reporter with USA Today's Deep South Connect team. Find her on X @IreneEWright or email her at ismith@usatodayco.com.

title: Maine lifeguard "started swimming like hell" when shark pulled him underwater
description: A lifeguard said a shark off the coast of Scarborough Beach in Maine grabbed onto his buoy and pulled him 5 feet underwater before he was able to get free.
fullText:
A lifeguard in Maine said he "started swimming like hell" when a shark grabbed onto his buoy and pulled him underwater off the coast of Scarborough Beach on Saturday.

Greg Wilfert said he initially thought he was caught in the propeller of a boat.

"'Cause that's the only thing I could think of until I realized there was no boat," he said.

Wilfert said he was pulled about 5 feet underwater before he was able to get free and emerge on shore unharmed.

"It was frightening," he said. "I'm not going to deny that."

Officials along the East Coast say there are more sharks closer to shore in areas where they don't usually go.

Since last week, at least a dozen sharks have been spotted close to popular beaches in the area of Wilfert's encounter, according to Scarborough's marine resources officer Daryen Granata.

"Usually we'll see one or two here and there. This is a large volume, larger than I've seen, and I've worked this area for 30-plus years," Granata said.

The trend is happening as conservation efforts have led to an increase in marine life populations in recent years, experts say.

"We're gonna see more of everything, including more sharks," OCEARCH founder Chris Fischer explained.

His nonprofit studies sharks by catching, tagging and collecting data before releasing them back into the ocean.

"It means just try to be a little bit more aware of what's going on in the environment around you. You see a lot of life, steer clear of that," he warned.

Still, shark encounters remain rare. Last year, the International Shark Attack File reported 25 unprovoked bites.

title: Oklahoma victim fights back after teen charged in rapes walks free — as feds could storm in: attorney
description: Rachel Bussett says one victim's family is pursuing civil litigation after Jesse Mack Butler walked free on 11 counts including rape charges.
fullText:
An Oklahoma teenager accused of sexually assaulting and strangling two high school girls walked free without serving a day in prison, spurring public outrage as a victim's family prepares to fight back.

"We're moving on to the next phase, which is civil litigation," Rachel Bussett, an attorney representing the family of one girl in the case, told Fox News Digital.

Jesse Mack Butler was initially charged as an adult at 17 with counts including attempted first-degree rape, rape by instrumentation, sexual battery, forcible oral sodomy, and domestic assault and battery by strangulation. But he ultimately received youthful-offender status and pleaded no contest to all 11 counts in August 2025.

Oklahoma Teen Accused Of Raping Two Girls Walks Free; Da Furiously Calls In Feds: 'Made My Blood Boil'

Instead of being sent to prison, he was placed under the supervision of the Oklahoma Office of Juvenile Affairs and ordered to complete a rehabilitation plan. Once Butler reached age 19 at midnight on Aug. 4, the court's jurisdiction lapsed, and the case was dismissed by operation of law.

For the family she represents, Bussett said, the outcome was painful but hardly unexpected.

"They were sad and upset, obviously, because they didn't want the deal to go through this way, but they weren't surprised," Bussett said. "They knew that it was going to happen from the beginning."

The family may now have two possible paths forward.

80% Of Claims In America's Largest Sexual Abuse Settlement In History Could Be Fraudulent, La Da Says

Bussett said the family is preparing for civil litigation while also hoping federal authorities take a fresh look at the case.

She said her understanding is that materials are being referred for review to determine whether content allegedly found on Butler's phone could qualify as child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and whether it was distributed. Bussett said her client had seen material she believes was on the phone.

"We know that that's a long shot," Bussett said of possible federal action, "but we're holding confident in the process."

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Department of Justice for additional information on the case.

Follow The Fox True Crime Team On X

Bussett also blasted her client's treatment during the earlier prosecution, describing an encounter with the former elected district attorney that she characterized as a "mock cross-examination."

Bussett said the teen believed she was speaking with someone she could trust to protect her, only to feel "absolutely attacked."

"Not only are they often not believed, but then they're attacked by those who are supposed to help them," Bussett said of sexual-assault victims coming forward.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the previous district attorney for comment.

Like What You're Reading? Click Here For More

Beyond the family's troubling encounters with public officials, Butler's defense attorney, Derek Chance, drew further criticism at the hearing after suggesting Butler was innocent and had been victimized by the case, according to newly elected Payne and Logan County District Attorney Jeremiah Gregory.

"Today's hearing included disingenuous assertions from the defense regarding the defendant's innocence, that he was the victim in this matter and that the victim's assertions were false and had no bearing. The defense portrayed that somehow the perpetrator suffered more than these victims. What was said was insincere, untruthful and an affront to these victims and what they have endured," Gregory said in a statement.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"Nothing has made my blood boil more."

WATCH: Police bodycam shows arrest of Oklahoma teen Jesse Butler

Gregory said constitutional double jeopardy protections bar Oklahoma from prosecuting Butler a second time, and he has contacted the appropriate federal agency to request a prosecutorial review of the case.

"I cannot undo what has already been done," Gregory said, "but I can — and will — continue to stand as a strong voice for all victims of violent crime."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Payne and Logan County District Attorney's Office, the Oklahoma Office of Juvenile Affairs and Butler's attorney for additional comment.

title: Democratic senators question Belgian diamond industry about ring given to Trump
description: Two Democratic senators are demanding answers from two Belgian firms about an 18-carat gold ring encrusted with 321 diamonds that was given to U.S.
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Aug 11 (Reuters) - Two Democratic senators are demanding answers from two Belgian firms about an 18-carat gold ring encrusted with 321 diamonds that was ‌given to U.S. President Donald Trump weeks before the U.S. exempted Europe's diamond industry ‌from new tariffs.

• In an August 10 letter to the Antwerp World Diamond Centre and David ​Gotlib Luxury Cufflinks, Senators Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut warned that the gift raised serious legal questions under U.S. federal bribery law and could result in criminal penalties for the companies.

• "At best, your (gift to) ... President Trump amidst high-stakes tariff decisions creates the glaring appearance of impropriety. ‌At worst, it reinforces that foreign ⁠corporate special interests can … buy lucrative tariff exemptions simply by showering President Trump with shiny gifts," they wrote in the letter.

• The senators said the ⁠ring, handcrafted by David Gotlib, was presented to the U.S. ambassador in Belgium by the president of the Antwerp World Diamond Centre on June 28 as a gift for Trump in honor of the ​250th anniversary ​of the U.S.

• On July 24, the Trump ​administration officially exempted European natural diamonds from ‌new Section 301 tariffs, restoring the Belgian diamond industry's prior zero-percent tariff access.

• The senators asked the firms to respond to a series of questions by August 24, including the value of the ring, who paid for it, and any discussions about tariffs with the Trump administration before the exemption was announced.

• Media reports have put the value of the ring at $25,000 to $35,000.

• Republicans ‌control both houses of Congress now, but Reuters reported ​last week that Democrats are developing a broad investigative ​strategy targeting companies and financial firms surrounding ​Trump if they return to power after congressional elections in November.

• The ‌White House denied any favors to special ​interests. A spokesman said the ​decision to exempt the diamond industry from new tariffs merely upheld the Trump administration's previous agreement to provide preferential treatment for diamonds under the U.S.-European Union trade deal signed ​in Scotland last July.

• An ‌administration official said the diamond ring was federal property, and if the president wanted ​to keep it, he would have to pay the government market price for ​it.

title: O’Reilly on Trump pressuring Iran toward a deal: ‘I don’t think he’s flailing’
description: Political commentator Bill O’Reilly on Monday said Trump is not “flailing” as he seeks to pressure Iran to accept a deal to end the conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz while also addressing the r...
fullText:
Political commentator Bill O'Reilly on Monday said Trump is not "flailing" as he seeks to pressure Iran to accept a deal to end the conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz while also addressing the regime's nuclear program.

When asked about Trump's policy, O'Reilly advised that the president needs to inflict "more pain on Iran than Iran is inflicting on the world." In response, NewsNation's Leland Vittert pressed the commentator on whether Trump was "flailing."

"I don't think he's flailing," O'Reilly told the "On Balance" host. "I don't think that's fair. He's got to make very difficult decisions. He didn't want to kill thousands of civilians. He told me that directly, all right? He didn't want to do it."

"But now there doesn't seem to be any other choice. So these mullahs aren't going to stop. And when somebody isn't going to stop, you have to stop them," he continued. "And the only way we can stop them is to destroy the infrastructure of their country, which includes the uranium at Pickaxe and the capital city. You do that, the equation changes."

O'Reilly added that if he were president, he would "take out" and "obliterate" Pickaxe Mountain and then tell citizens in Tehran to evacuate "because we're going to wreck your infrastructure."

"That means water. That means power," he continued. "Now, the world would go crazy. You know what would happen. [The] Democratic Party would jump up and down here. Trump would be almost alone. But that is the way to do it."

Vittert indicated that Trump appears to be "paralyzed" between not launching new attacks and not being able to bring the Islamic Republic back to the negotiating table. O'Reilly disagreed, saying the U.S. "had enough" with Germany and Japan during World War II "and we took care of that."

"And we're going to have to do the same thing with Iran," he continued, later saying that Trump "is not flailing, he just has to change the game plan."

The commander in chief's latest demand from Iran is to have the regime pay for damages to the U.S., referring to the 2000 attack on the USS Cole. This compensation could go to the families of the protesters who were killed in Iran "over the last 50 years, not to mention the 52,000 that have been killed in the last five months."

Trump added that, moving forward, the compensation requirement would be part of ongoing negotiations.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baqaei told reporters in Iran on Monday that there are no talks currently happening between the two countries, the state-run Fars News Agency reported. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said early Tuesday that Tehran has proven itself to be "resilient" and an "invincible power against the U.S.," according to the local outlet.

"In diplomacy as well, the Iranian nation showed that it knows how to defend its rights properly," Araghchi continued. "Various officials have repeatedly told us that 'you won both the war and the diplomacy.'"

title: John Gotti’s grandson kept trying to delay prison to donate kidney to mother. A judge said enough.
description: Late mob boss John Gotti ’s reality TV star grandson has reported to federal prison after trying to stave off his sentence on fraud charges by saying he was going to donate a kidney to his ailing moth...
fullText:
NEW YORK (AP) — Late mob boss John Gotti 's reality TV star grandson has reported to federal prison after trying to stave off his sentence on fraud charges by saying he was going to donate a kidney to his ailing mother, Victoria Gotti.

The Federal Bureau of Prisons confirmed Tuesday that Carmine Agnello began his 15-month prison term the previous day at the Federal Correctional Institution Fairton in southern New Jersey.

Agnello, who starred on " Growing Up Gotti " in the mid-2000s, was originally scheduled to report to prison in July. But U.S. District Court Judge Nusrat Choudhury agreed to delay that until Sept. 18, saying it would allow enough time to recover from the surgery, presuming that happened by Aug. 10 as Agnello suggested

Agnello's lawyers have said in court filings that Victoria Gotti, the daughter of the former head of New York's Gambino crime family, suffers from chronic kidney disease.

On Monday, though, with no operation in sight, Choudhury ordered Agnello to surrender immediately to federal authorities.

"Because there is no concrete evidence that an organ transplant will be scheduled to take place at any time between today and Sept. 18, 2026, the request for another deferral of Mr. Agnello's self-surrender is unjustified," the judge said.

Agnello lawyer Robert Beltrani said in a letter that surgeons needed more time to set a date for the operation because Gotti was dealing with infections.

"It is undisputed that Carmine is a great match for Ms. Gotti," he said. "He is simply asking the Court to allow him to remain available to his mother during this very limited period while her doctors determine whether and when she can proceed with transplant."

Prosecutors objected, noting that a medical report attached to the defendant's letter said doctors were working to "identify the etiology and the proper treatment" for Gotti's recurring infections and no transplant could happen until they are fully treated.

"Clearly, the transplant surgery is not imminent," said Joseph Nocella, U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of New York.

Nocella's office declined to comment further, and lawyers for Agnello did not immediately respond to email messages. Nor did Gotti, an author and former columnist for the New York Post.

Agnello pleaded guilty in 2024 to wire fraud after prosecutors said he fraudulently obtained $1.1 million in loans from a federal program meant to help small businesses during the COVID-19 pandemic.

A resident of Long Island, he obtained the loans on behalf of his company, Crown Auto Parts & Recycling LLC, but lied about how many people it employed, his criminal record and his plans for the funds, prosecutors said.

The company ceased operations before Agnello applied for the loan, which he ultimately used on other ventures including a $420,000 investment in a cryptocurrency business, prosecutors said.

Agnello, now 40, was a teen when he and his brothers briefly rose to fame sporting gel-spiked hairdos on "Growing up Gotti," which followed the family's life on Long Island.

His grandfather earned the nicknames "Teflon Don" and "Dapper Don" for his flamboyant style and ability to beat some of the criminal charges he faced over the years. He died in a Missouri federal prison in 2002 at age 61.

The New Jersey lockup where Agnello is now incarcerated has housed some notable inmates over the years.

Most recently disgraced former New York Congressman George Santos served less than three months of a more than seven-year sentence there before President Donald Trump granted him clemency last year.

Follow Philip Marcelo at https://x.com/philmarcelo

title: China bets on AI weather forecasting as extreme weather intensifies
description: As meteorologists tracked Typhoon Dolphin's path toward China in recent days, a new generation of artificial intelligence weather models
fullText:
SHANGHAI, Aug 11 (Reuters) - As meteorologists tracked Typhoon Dolphin's path toward China in recent days, a new generation of artificial intelligence weather models worked alongside traditional forecasting systems, highlighting ‌China's emergence as a leading player in the race to improve weather prediction.

Chinese-developed systems, including Shanghai AI Laboratory-developed ‌Fengwu, Huawei's Pangu and Fudan University's Fuxi, are among a handful of AI forecasting models that researchers say can generate forecasts much faster than conventional systems while ​matching or surpassing them on some measures of accuracy.

For decades, weather prediction has relied on numerical models running on supercomputers that simulate atmospheric physics. AI models instead learn patterns from vast archives of historical weather observations and can produce forecasts in a fraction of the time. The technology is increasingly being tested during typhoon season in East Asia, where even small improvements in track ‌forecasts can help authorities better prepare for ⁠flooding, organise evacuations and manage potential transport disruptions.

The rise of AI weather forecasting has created a new arena of competition among technology companies, research institutes and meteorological agencies, with China emerging as ⁠one of the field's leading players.

Among the best-known AI forecasting systems globally are Google's GraphCast and GenCast, Nvidia-backed FourCastNet and the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts' AI Forecasting System, known as AIFS.

Fengwu attracted attention after developers reported it outperformed GraphCast across ​roughly ​80% of evaluated weather variables and extended skilful global medium-range forecasts ​beyond 10 days.

"With more extreme weather, people need information ‌to make decisions, both local governments, the national government, also the average person, farmers and fisherman," said Sun Zhi, the CTO of Techwind, the company responsible for Fengwu's industrial applications. "So we want to help provide better information so people can make decisions."

While AI systems are becoming an increasingly important complement to conventional forecasting because of their speed and lower computing costs, they are unlikely to fully replace traditional weather models in the near future.

According to Techwind's Sun, AI models are already ‌capable of predicting the path of typhoons — five days out from Dolphin's ​landfall Fengwu predicted the time and place it would hit mainland China ​to within 30 minutes and 30 km (19 miles) — but ​they still lag conventional weather forecasts in predicting the intensity of a storm and they ‌are still untested predicting major climate developments.

"If we predict ​a climate change event 18 ​months in advance, people won't believe it," Sun said. "They need to know it's reliable. We need to do years of scientific research before people trust us when we say there will be an El Nino event or ​we say the changing temperature on the ‌sea's surface will affect the breeding cycle of fish."

As the tech forecasters work to make their systems ever ​more sophisticated, the concurrent use of both methods is likely to continue for some time.

title: Socialist Wisconsin governor candidate referred to America as 'abundance of suffering,' resurfaced post shows
description: Fox News Digital found Francesca Hong's X posts calling America "an abundance of suffering" and urging police abolition in her governor campaign.
fullText:
A socialist candidate for governor in Wisconsin with an extensive history of inflammatory online posts once described America as "an abundance of suffering," Fox News Digital has found.

"I want this country to stop being an abundance of suffering but a wealth of opportunity," reads a Jan. 20, 2022 X post from Wisconsin state Rep. Francesca Hong, who is running in the Democratic Party's primary election to become the state's top official.

"We can do this by providing equal rights to Black and Brown folks," the post continues. "Elect more Black and Brown folks who won't be racist obstructionists. We can all be better and do so much more."

Socialist Frontrunner In The Hot Seat After 'Cancel Thanksgiving' Post Emerges Online

This isn't the first time the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) candidate has faced scrutiny for past comments on social media that are especially critical of America and its institutions and ideals.

"Cancel Thanksgiving. Should have done this in 1621," Hong wrote in a now-deleted post on X.

"If it takes a worldwide pandemic for us to realize we should stop celebrating colonialism and the original superspreader event that killed indigenous folx [sic] and women, so be it," she added, referring to the spread of smallpox that killed many indigenous Americans.

Despite a string of posts, the former chef and mother-of-one, is now running for the Democratic nomination for governor in Wisconsin. She's the latest in a strong of socialists seeking statewide or federal office in this year's primary against establishment Democrats.

Left's Latest Socialist Darling Dragged Over 'Whiteness' Comments Pulling In Her Own Family: 'Weirdo Racism'

Hong, who is Korean America, also said in a 2019 post that she was anxious in the company of White people.

"I ate two bites of my kid's cheeseburger at a Culver's in black river falls and told him they ran out of ice cream," that post said. "Mostly just wanted to leave bc I was on the verge of a anxiety attack...to (sic) many old white people who didn't think we spoke english."

When prosecutors declined to press charges in 2021 for the high-profile shooting of Jacob Blake in August 2020, in Kenosha, Wisc., Hong joined the chorus of left-wing voicing calling to abolish police.

"How is 7 bullets in the back not excessive force," she said at the time. "Police exist to uphold White supremacy. Defund then abolish. Reform can't be an option. My heart breaks for the trauma the Blake family and their community continues to endure."

Top Wisconsin Democratic Socialist Candidate Confronted On Past 'Defund Police' Rhetoric

Hong's team declined in July to walk back her position on police.

"Rep. Hong has spoken in the past about police and prison abolition as an aspirational goal, akin to eradicating disease or eliminating poverty," a spokesperson told Fox News Digital at the time. "Her values haven't changed, but the way she talks about this issue has."

Hong has acknowledged that the governor does not have the power to defund the police.

The candidate brushed off the scrutiny of her posts when asked about them by Fox News Digital ahead of her primary election on Tuesday, saying she wanted to be a sports journalist in college.

"I learned then you have some hot takes, and sometimes bad takes on Twitter, and I let my feelings out into the world," Hong said.

Francesca Hong Asked About Lack Of Aoc Endorsement And The House Dem's Remark About The 'Woke 1' Era

She said she was focused on issues voters are concerned about.

Hong's campaign did not return a request for comment on the latest post uncovered by Fox News Digital.

Fox News' CJ Womack and Paul Steinhouser contributed to this report.
